title: Exploring the Investigative World of Science

standard_text: Investigating like a scientist: asking testable questions, planning fair investigations with independent, dependent and controlled variables, sampling and repeating measurements, recording data in tables and graphs, observations and inferences, and drawing evidence-based conclusions (summary of NCERT Curiosity Chapter 1).
meta_desc: Free CBSE Class 8 Science worksheets for NCERT Curiosity Chapter 1: planning investigations, independent, dependent and controlled variables, repeat readings and averages, observations and inferences, and graphs. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Change one variable, measure another, keep the rest the same.
key_sub: Repeat, average and look for patterns.
body_html:
How to think about it

A scientific investigation starts with a testable question. In a fair test we change one variable on purpose (the independent variable), measure what happens (the dependent variable) and keep everything else the same (controlled variables). Repeating measurements and using bigger samples make results more reliable.

We record data in tables and graphs and look for patterns. An observation is what we notice directly; an inference is what we conclude from it. Conclusions must be based on evidence, and other scientists check the work before it is accepted.

Example

More turns, more pins picked up. Independent variable?

the thing changed on purpose

Answer: the number of turns

Example

Readings 14, 15, 16 s. Average?

45 ÷ 3

Answer: 15 s

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up the independent and dependent variables.
  • Changing two variables at once.
  • Calling an inference an observation.

faq.q: What is the difference between independent and dependent variables?
faq.a: The independent variable is changed on purpose; the dependent variable is measured to see how it responds.
Repeating and averaging reduces the effect of random errors and makes results more reliable.

items.q: A student measures the time for 20 swings of a pendulum three times: 42 s, 38 s, 40 s. What is the average?
Which of these is an observation rather than an inference?
c: the leaves on the plant are drooping
items.e: An observation is what we notice directly.

items.q: Why do scientists use units such as metres and seconds?
c: so that everyone understands and can compare measurements
items.e: SI units are used all over the world.

items.q: What are controlled variables?
c: the things kept the same so the test is fair
items.e: Pot size and amount of water could be controlled.

items.q: Why do scientists keep a record of every step of an investigation?
c: so that it can be checked and repeated by others
so nobody else can do it
items.e: Records also help find mistakes.

items.q: A student measures the time for a ball to roll down a ramp three times: 11 s, 11 s, 14 s. What is the average?
Why should an investigation be safe?
c: to avoid harm to people, animals and the environment
items.e: Wear goggles and follow your teacher.

items.q: A student measures the mass of a potato three times: 29 g, 30 g, 31 g. What is the average?
Why is it useful to make a prediction before an experiment?
c: it gives a clear idea to test
items.e: A wrong prediction still teaches us something.

items.q: What is an anomaly in a set of results?
c: a result that does not fit the pattern of the others
items.e: Check how it happened.

items.q: Which is a good way to compare the number of students who like different fruits?
items.e: Bar graphs compare categories.

items.q: A student measures the mass of a potato three times: 20 g, 22 g, 18 g. What is the average?
What is the first thing to do when planning an investigation?
c: decide the question to be answered
items.e: A clear question guides the plan.

items.q: A student measures the temperature of water in a pot three times: 36 °C, 34 °C, 38 °C. What is the average?
A student measures the temperature of water in a pot three times: 44 °C, 46 °C, 45 °C. What is the average?
A student measures the mass of a potato three times: 16 g, 18 g, 20 g. What is the average?
A student measures the height of a bean plant three times: 25 cm, 23 cm, 24 cm. What is the average?
Which of these questions can be investigated scientifically?
c: Does adding salt change the boiling point of water?
items.e: It can be answered by measuring.

items.q: What do we call a simplified picture or object that explains how something works?
items.e: A globe is a model of the Earth.

items.q: What should be done with results that do not fit the pattern?
c: check them carefully and repeat the measurement if possible
items.e: Odd results may show a mistake or something new.

items.q: Investigation: Do bread moulds grow faster in warm places? What is the independent variable?
c: the type and size of bread
the area covered by mould after three days
items.e: Independent: the temperature. Dependent: the area covered by mould after three days. Controlled: the type and size of bread.

items.q: Investigation: Does the mass of an object change the stretch of a spring? What is the dependent variable?
c: the colour of the student's shirt
the mass hung on the spring
items.e: Independent: the mass hung on the spring. Dependent: the length of the spring. Controlled: the type of spring.

items.q: Investigation: Does the surface change how far a toy car rolls? What is the independent variable?
items.e: Independent: the type of surface. Dependent: the distance the car rolls. Controlled: the slope of the ramp.

items.q: Investigation: Does the number of turns in a coil change the strength of an electromagnet? What is the independent variable?
c: the number of pins it picks up
the current and the iron core
the colour of the student's shirt
items.e: Independent: the number of turns. Dependent: the number of pins it picks up. Controlled: the current and the iron core.

items.q: Investigation: Does the mass of an object change the stretch of a spring? Which should be a controlled variable?
c: the colour of the student's shirt
the mass hung on the spring
items.e: Independent: the mass hung on the spring. Dependent: the length of the spring. Controlled: the type of spring.

items.q: What is an inference?
c: a conclusion drawn from observations and reasoning
items.e: Wet ground is an observation; 'it rained' is an inference.

items.q: Investigation: Does a salt solution conduct electricity better when more salt is added? Which should be a controlled variable?
items.e: Independent: the amount of salt. Dependent: the brightness of the bulb. Controlled: the amount of water.

items.q: Investigation: Does the colour of light change how fast a pond plant gives off bubbles? Which should be a controlled variable?

items.e: Independent: the colour of the light. Dependent: the number of bubbles per minute. Controlled: the distance of the lamp.
